1:
The date is worked closely. Gill puts it in the sixth year of the captivity, in the month answering to late summer, corrects the versions reading a fifth month, and thinks the day a sabbath; Wesley supposes the elders came to keep the day or to ask what would become of their brethren. Keil and Delitzsch measure the interval at a year and two months from the call and set out the sequence: idolatry seen, the city smitten, the sanctuary forsaken. Henry makes the same calculation and explains why a man in Babylon is shown Jerusalem: captives reckoned their peace and trouble by the city's.

Clarke admires the device by which idolatry is personified and made an idol, named from the provocation it gives. Ellicott infers from the opening line that a priest already known as a prophet was held in regard among the exiles and had a house of his own, and explains the elders' title by who the captives mostly were. Calvin insists what kind of event this is: the man did not move, and only seemed to himself seized by the Spirit.

The figure divides them. Gill reports versions reading a likeness of a man where the text has fire, and thinks the human form implied by loins and a hand. Ellicott denies this is the earlier vision returning, since that bursts on the prophet later inside the temple, and notes how carefully likeness, appearance and form are repeated to keep it visionary. Calvin rejects the rendering that makes the last word angel, since it means colour, and cannot fix which beyond the received opinion of amber. Wesley identifies the figure with the man seen on the throne and hears wrath in the fire.

The carrying off is figurative. Ellicott says the prophet never left Chaldea, as a later verse shows, and identifies the gate as the northern one leading up from the people's court to the priests', by which they went straight to the altar. Calvin says the same of the hand, a likeness and not a hand, and warns against imagining a real journey between earth and sky. Gill takes the hand for the Spirit sent by Christ; Wesley marks the passage down to the sixteenth verse as vision only.

What the image was nobody knows. Clarke lists a Baal set up by an apostate king, the god of war, or the youth beloved by the goddess of love, and gives the case for the last, since that youth was killed by a boar sent in jealousy by the goddess's other lover, which fits the name exactly. Wesley takes the plainer view, an idol set up, destroyed and set up again by successive reigns, and explains the name from the affront to a God who had married the nation to himself. He and Ellicott connect the northern position with an altar moved that way by an earlier king, likely how the gate got its name; Keil and Delitzsch reason from the prophet's station that the image stood outside the entrance.

That the glory should be standing there is the sharpest stroke. Gill says the presence had not withdrawn though provoked, and an idol set where God himself was measures the insolence. Ellicott distinguishes it from the old glory filling the house, calling it the vision of the plain seen again, a vision within a vision; Calvin treats the reappearance as a seal on the message, arming a man with hard heads to deal with. On the threat, Ellicott notes a bare infinitive with no subject, so it might mean the removal of the people, but prefers the removal of God from his own sanctuary as truer to the vision, since what had to be broken was the confidence that a national God would defend his house whatever was done in it. Wesley adds that nobody intended it, though nothing else could be expected.
7:
Henry notices the method of the disclosure. The prophet is not set down at once in the chamber of images but led toward it by stages, partly so that he should have to search the thing out for himself and partly so that he should feel how carefully such discoveries have to be made. Ellicott cannot fix the place: it is clearly not where the prophet had been standing, and since he is later taken to the north gate of the outer enclosure this must lie somewhere between, though the older building record names no courts beyond the inner and the outer. Gill reports the identification with the eastern gate, the commonest entrance and the one where the council sat, so that what the prophet sees is their own chamber painted round with figures.

The digging is treated as part of the point. Clarke notes that the hole was too small to see through and had to be enlarged before anything could be observed. Calvin makes the whole action visionary and reads its meaning off the geography: an idol in one part of the temple would have been intolerable, but a defilement running through every part of it shows a people past recovery. Wesley identifies what the opening leads to as a private door by which the priests went in to their images.

What is painted there settles the question of origin. Clarke lists the likely subjects, the ox and ape and dog, the crocodile, the ibis and the beetle, and compares the walls of tombs in that country where such figures still appear. Ellicott agrees the rites are Egyptian and argues the case carefully: creature worship existed elsewhere, and painting idols on walls is elsewhere credited to a Chaldean import, but the combination here is thoroughly Egyptian and the politics of the moment point the same way. Gill takes the creeping things for beetles and the like worshipped as gods, and Wesley for whatever the neighbouring nations adored.

The worshippers are named, and the number is disputed. Ellicott doubts that any chamber about the courts could actually have held seventy men, and reminds the reader that a scene given in vision for instruction need not be possible in every detail; he denies that these were the council, which did not exist until after the return, and refers the number instead to the seventy who once went up with Moses. Calvin agrees the standing seventy of the old constitution are not meant, and takes the word for elders as an office rather than an age, while allowing that the number alludes to that order. Wesley calls them heads of tribes and families who should have been examples and were ringleaders, and observes of the one man named that his father had been forward in a reformation while the son is as forward in corruption; Clarke identifies the father as an officer of the temple whose place the son probably inherited, and puts him at the head of the band.

Secrecy is what makes the offence particular. Ellicott distinguishes it from the ordinary idolatry of the nation, which worshipped a supposed deity through images and did so openly enough; here the creature itself was worshipped through paintings, and that was done in the dark, which explains the difficulty of getting at the place. Gill treats the doubled question as a demand that the prophet weigh what he has seen, and Calvin explains why the question is put to him at all, that he may pass sentence as a judge and leave the guilty without plea; Calvin also notes that the men are not named out of any respect but reproved the harder, since a corruption that starts with elders drags everyone after it. Wesley states the excuse the worshippers gave themselves, that a God who does not see them is a God they may replace.
13:
The tour runs on a formula: each stop is announced as worse than the last. Matthew Henry notes that the prophet had seen enough already and is twice told to turn again; those who live retired, he says, do not know what wickedness the world holds. John Wesley offers two readings of the comparative: the later sins are greater because added to the rest, or because some circumstance makes them so — and he settles on place, these being done on holier ground.

The second stop is the northern gate of the house. John Gill identifies it as the one little used of several, and observes that idolatry told worse where the Lord was most solemnly served. Wesley places it at the outer court, so called because women were admitted. Keil and Delitzsch draw the contrast that organises the vision: the men, represented by the seventy, worshipped in secret chambers, while the women sat at the temple gate and mourned in public.

Who Tammuz was divides the voices. Keil and Delitzsch report that Jerome, with Melito and the Greek fathers, read the name as Adonis, and treat that as correct. Adam Clarke follows it, adding the report that the Lebanon stream ran red at the festival — ochre in swollen water, he explains, not sympathy. Charles Ellicott explains why the Greek name could not stand here: in Hebrew form it means Lord and is used of God. John Calvin dissents. He doubts the rite reached Judaea, the lamentation being attested in Greece and Asia Minor rather than the neighbouring regions, and prefers Osiris, wept for yearly by the Egyptians, whose neighbours the Jews were and from whom they had taken other rites.

Calvin treats the scene as a sin peculiar to women, and Henry agrees: the mourners shed idolatrous tears at the very door in defiance of the sacred rites, and both he and Clarke report debasing practices going with the mourning. Calvin's point is the depth reached — women taught the law from childhood carried past all moderation.

The last stop is the inner court, into which Gill says none but priests might come. Clarke and Ellicott give the same account of the five and twenty: heads of the twenty-four courses with the high priest, standing for the priesthood as the elders stood for the people. Ellicott presses the wording — not about but as it were, a phrase belonging to vision — and both he and Keil and Delitzsch fix the spot between porch and altar as the court's most sacred ground. Calvin takes the number as a round one for an uncertain, and refuses to make the sin one of error: the law forbidding this worship gave its reason, that the lights were made for our service, so that making a servant a god was known to be preposterous. Heaviest for him is the posture — the turned back, not denial merely but contempt, as though God were unworthy of regard. Wesley reads it the same way.

The branch at the nose defeats everyone. Clarke takes it for boughs carried in procession, and refuses the filthier constructions. Ellicott calls it an allusion to a lost custom and offers the Parsee habit of holding twigs before the mouth as the simplest guess; Wesley compares the wreathed staff of the wine-god's worshippers. Calvin turns to the violence filling the land, taking the word as a part standing for every breach of the second table, and finds the intolerable thing in the order: having despised men, they attacked God. The sentence answers — fury, an eye that will not spare, no hearing of the loud cry. Ellicott reads it as the day of grace outrun, the chapter's chief lesson. Calvin guards the point: prayer springing from faith is never rejected, but what is described here is the tumult necessity wrings from unbelief, and the elect are excepted.
